examples.description: Attribution: a join between two streams. Both sides are streams, so the engine keeps state for each side and emits a row when a pair matches.
examples.sql:
SELECT c.click_id, i.impression_id, i.campaign_id, i.placement, i.user_id, i.cost_micros,
       i.impression_time, c.click_time
FROM ad_impression AS i
JOIN ad_click AS c
  ON c.impression_id = i.impression_id
 AND c.user_id = i.user_id
 AND c.click_time BETWEEN i.impression_time AND i.impression_time + INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
examples.title: Attribution: a join between two streams

examples.description: Clicks per campaign, per five minutes: a window over a join. The same join, grouped into five-minute windows of click time. It is written over the two streams rather than over `attributed_clicks`, because a continuous query is written over declared streams.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(c.click_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE) AS window_end,
  i.campaign_id,
  COUNT(*)                  AS clicks,
  COUNT(DISTINCT i.user_id) AS clicking_users
FROM ad_impression AS i
JOIN ad_click AS c
  ON c.impression_id = i.impression_id
 AND c.user_id = i.user_id
 AND c.click_time BETWEEN i.impression_time AND i.impression_time + INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
GROUP BY TUMBLE(c.click_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE), i.campaign_id
examples.title: Clicks per campaign, per five minutes: a window over a join

examples.description: Impressions per campaign, per five minutes (Click attribution)
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(impression_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE) AS window_end,
  campaign_id,
  COUNT(*)         AS impressions,
  SUM(cost_micros) AS spend_micros
FROM ad_impression
GROUP BY TUMBLE(impression_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE), campaign_id
examples.title: Impressions per campaign, per five minutes

examples.description: Card authorisation velocity. A card is used four times in ninety seconds, at four different merchants, in a country the cardholder has never transacted in. Each authorisation on its own is unremarkable. The *pattern* is the fraud, and it exists only in the relationship between events that arrive milliseconds apart.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(a.auth_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE) AS window_end,
  a.card_id,
  h.risk_band,
  COUNT(*)                      AS auth_count,
  SUM(a.amount_minor)           AS total_minor,
  COUNT(DISTINCT a.merchant_id) AS distinct_merchants
FROM card_auth AS a
LEFT JOIN cardholder FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF a.auth_time AS h
       ON a.card_id = h.card_id
WHERE a.status = 'APPROVED'
GROUP BY TUMBLE(a.auth_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE), a.card_id, h.risk_band
examples.title: Card authorisation velocity

examples.description: Sequencing run QC. A sequencing run takes hours and costs real money. Somewhere in hour two, one sample's coverage collapses — a bad library prep, a clogged flow cell lane. If you find out when the run finishes and the pipeline reports, you have paid for the whole run and you rerun the sample tomorrow. If you find out in hour two, you stop, fix and restart.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(r.called_at, INTERVAL '30' SECOND) AS window_end,
  r.run_id,
  r.sample_id,
  m.panel,
  COUNT(*)                    AS read_count,
  AVG(r.depth)                AS mean_depth,
  MIN(r.mapping_quality)      AS min_mapq,
  COUNT(DISTINCT r.target_id) AS targets_touched
FROM read_metric AS r
LEFT JOIN sample_manifest FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF r.called_at AS m
       ON r.sample_id = m.sample_id
WHERE r.mapping_quality >= 30
GROUP BY TUMBLE(r.called_at, INTERVAL '30' SECOND), r.run_id, r.sample_id, m.panel
examples.title: Sequencing run QC

examples.description: The funnel. One row per five minutes, step and device, keyed by all three — key columns `[0, 1, 2]`. `COUNT(DISTINCT session_id)` rather than `COUNT(*)`: a shopper who presses "pay" twice is one session that reached payment, not two.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(event_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE) AS window_end,
  step,
  device,
  COUNT(*)                   AS events,
  COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions,
  SUM(basket_minor)          AS basket_minor
FROM checkout_event
GROUP BY TUMBLE(event_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE), step, device
examples.title: The funnel

examples.description: Payment-failure spikes. `WHERE` narrows the rows before they are grouped; `HAVING` narrows the groups after. The view holds only windows worth paging somebody about — so a subscriber to it is an alerting rule, with nothing to filter on its side.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(event_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE) AS window_end,
  device,
  COUNT(*)          AS failures,
  SUM(basket_minor) AS basket_at_risk_minor
FROM checkout_event
WHERE step = 'PAYMENT_FAILED'
GROUP BY TUMBLE(event_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE), device
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
examples.title: Payment-failure spikes

examples.description: Intraday counterparty exposure. A treasury desk pays out all day. Each payment is small against the balance sheet; the question that matters is how much has gone to *one counterparty* since the day opened, against the limit that counterparty was granted. Answer it a minute late and you have already breached.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(s.value_time, INTERVAL '1' HOUR) AS window_end,
  s.counterparty_id,
  s.currency,
  c.rating,
  COUNT(*)              AS payment_count,
  SUM(s.amount_minor)   AS outgoing_minor,
  MAX(s.amount_minor)   AS largest_minor
FROM settlement AS s
LEFT JOIN counterparty FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF s.value_time AS c
       ON s.counterparty_id = c.counterparty_id
WHERE s.direction = 'PAY'
GROUP BY TUMBLE(s.value_time, INTERVAL '1' HOUR), s.counterparty_id, s.currency, c.rating
examples.title: Intraday counterparty exposure

examples.description: Revenue per category per hour. A second aggregate, served as a view only. Not everything needs to be in the lake: the merchandising dashboard reads this one over Flight SQL.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(ordered_at, INTERVAL '1' HOUR) AS window_end,
  category,
  COUNT(*)          AS lines,
  SUM(amount_minor) AS revenue_minor
FROM order_line
GROUP BY TUMBLE(ordered_at, INTERVAL '1' HOUR), category
examples.title: Revenue per category per hour

examples.description: Revenue per region per hour — and into Iceberg. Keyed by `(window_end, region)` — `[0, 1]` — and registered writing to `hourly_revenue_table`. The SQL does not mention Iceberg: where an answer goes is the registration's business, so the same query could feed a view, a Kafka topic or a table without changing a word.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(ordered_at, INTERVAL '1' HOUR) AS window_end,
  region,
  COUNT(*)                    AS orders,
  SUM(amount_minor)           AS revenue_minor,
  COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers
FROM order_line
GROUP BY TUMBLE(ordered_at, INTERVAL '1' HOUR), region
examples.title: Revenue per region per hour — and into Iceberg

examples.description: Dispatches per depot per hour (Delivery SLA breaches)
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_START(dispatch_time, INTERVAL '1' HOUR) AS hour_start,
  depot,
  COUNT(*) AS dispatched
FROM dispatch
GROUP BY TUMBLE(dispatch_time, INTERVAL '1' HOUR), depot
examples.title: Dispatches per depot per hour

examples.description: Late deliveries: an interval join. The time bound *is* the SLA: a pair matches only if the delivery came between two and four hours after the dispatch. It also bounds the state — a dispatch can be forgotten four hours after it happened. Registered with `sink="sla_breaches"`, so every breach is appended to `data/sla_breaches.csv` as it is matched.
examples.sql:
SELECT d.shipment_id, d.depot, v.courier, d.dispatch_time, v.delivered_time
FROM dispatch AS d
JOIN delivery AS v
  ON v.shipment_id = d.shipment_id
 AND v.delivered_time BETWEEN d.dispatch_time + INTERVAL '2' HOUR AND d.dispatch_time + INTERVAL '4' HOUR
examples.title: Late deliveries: an interval join

examples.description: Undelivered: a `LEFT JOIN` that reports what did not happen. This is the query that sees an absence. A `LEFT JOIN` emits every dispatch: matched ones when their delivery arrives, and unmatched ones padded with nulls, once, when event time passes the end of the bound — four hours after dispatch — because only then can the engine know no delivery is coming. `WHERE v.shipment_id IS NULL` keeps only those.
examples.sql:
SELECT d.shipment_id, d.depot, d.dispatch_time
FROM dispatch AS d
LEFT JOIN delivery AS v
  ON v.shipment_id = d.shipment_id
 AND v.delivered_time BETWEEN d.dispatch_time AND d.dispatch_time + INTERVAL '4' HOUR
WHERE v.shipment_id IS NULL
  AND d.service = 'express'
examples.title: Undelivered: a `LEFT JOIN` that reports what did not happen

examples.description: Machine health, per minute. One row per machine per minute, keyed by `(window_end, machine_id)` — key columns `[0, 1]`. The window is what makes it safe to run for ever: a minute's state is released once it closes and its lateness has passed. Group by `machine_id` with no window and the engine refuses it (`PRV-2050`), because that state would grow with every machine for as long as the node runs.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(reading_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE) AS window_end,
  machine_id,
  line_id,
  COUNT(*)            AS readings,
  MIN(temperature_dc) AS min_temperature_dc,
  MAX(temperature_dc) AS max_temperature_dc,
  MAX(vibration_um)   AS max_vibration_um
FROM sensor_reading
GROUP BY TUMBLE(reading_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE), machine_id, line_id
examples.title: Machine health, per minute

examples.description: Overheat alarms, as they happen. No window, no state: a filter. It is registered with `sink="overheat_alerts"`, the binding under `pravaha.sinks` in the configuration, so every alarm is appended to `data/overheat_alerts.csv` as well as kept in the view.
examples.sql:
SELECT reading_id, machine_id, line_id, temperature_dc, reading_time
FROM sensor_reading
WHERE temperature_dc >= 950
examples.title: Overheat alarms, as they happen

examples.description: Large payments on foreign cards. Two filters, keyed by `payment_id` — `[0]`. Different `WHERE` clauses make them different plans, so they are separate computations with separate state. They are not separate reads of the topic.
examples.sql:
SELECT payment_id, merchant, card_country, amount_minor, paid_at
FROM payment
WHERE card_country <> 'GB' AND amount_minor >= 50000
examples.title: Large payments on foreign cards

examples.description: Declines (Many desks, one topic)
examples.sql:
SELECT payment_id, merchant, card_country, amount_minor, paid_at
FROM payment
WHERE status = 'DECLINED'
examples.title: Declines

examples.description: Each merchant's minutes, with an index on the merchant. This one is a statement rather than a bare `SELECT`, because it declares an index, and an index is a clause of the statement — there is no registration argument for it.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  TUMBLE_END(paid_at, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE) AS window_end,
  merchant,
  COUNT(*)          AS payments,
  SUM(amount_minor) AS amount_minor
FROM payment
WHERE status = 'APPROVED'
GROUP BY TUMBLE(paid_at, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE), merchant
examples.title: Each merchant's minutes, with an index on the merchant

examples.description: Lines at or under their reorder point. A filter comparing two columns of the same row. There is no window and no state beyond the view: because updates arrive as `-1`/`+1`, the view holds exactly the lines that are low *now*.
examples.sql:
SELECT sku, warehouse, on_hand, reorder_point, updated_at
FROM stock
WHERE on_hand <= reorder_point
examples.title: Lines at or under their reorder point

examples.description: The table, kept current. No filter and no aggregate: a keyed view of the table, `[0, 1]` — `(sku, warehouse)`. Every read of it is answered from the node's memory, so the buyers' questions never reach the database that runs the tills.
examples.sql:
SELECT sku, warehouse, on_hand, reorder_point, updated_at
FROM stock
examples.title: The table, kept current

examples.description: A sliding profile of every caller. `HOP(…, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE)` is a five-minute window that starts every minute, so each call belongs to five windows and "the last five minutes" is answered once a minute. A tumbling five-minute window would split a burst that straddles a boundary into two halves that each look innocent. Keyed by `(window_end, caller)` — `[0, 1]`.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  HOP_END(start_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE) AS window_end,
  caller,
  COUNT(*)               AS calls,
  COUNT(DISTINCT callee) AS distinct_callees,
  SUM(duration_s)        AS talk_seconds
FROM call_record
GROUP BY HOP(start_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE), caller
examples.title: A sliding profile of every caller

examples.description: Every long call to a premium destination. A filter, so no window and no state: each qualifying record is in the view as soon as it is read. The list of destinations is in the SQL because it changes rarely; when it changes, replace the query (Tutorial 3) and readers keep reading.
examples.sql:
SELECT cdr_id, caller, callee, callee_country, duration_s, start_time
FROM call_record
WHERE callee_country IN ('SB', 'TV', 'NU') AND duration_s >= 60
examples.title: Every long call to a premium destination

examples.description: The three busiest callers in each five minutes. `ROW_NUMBER() … WHERE rn <= 3` is the one ordering a continuous query supports: a maintained top-N. `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` over a stream are refused (`PRV-2020`) because they describe an order over rows that have not all arrived; a top-N per partition is incremental — a row entering the top three is emitted with its rank, the row it displaces is withdrawn.
examples.sql:
SELECT window_start, caller, calls, rn
FROM (
  SELECT window_start, caller, calls,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY window_start ORDER BY calls DESC) AS rn
  FROM (
    SELECT TUMBLE_START(start_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE) AS window_start, caller, COUNT(*) AS calls
    FROM call_record
    GROUP BY TUMBLE(start_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE), caller
  )
)
WHERE rn <= 3
examples.title: The three busiest callers in each five minutes

examples.description: The same feed, enriched. Two lookups, chained. Each trade is enriched from both tables as it passes; nothing is buffered and no window is needed, because a lookup join asks a question of a table rather than waiting for a matching event to arrive.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  t.trade_event_id,
  t.trade_id,
  t.product_type,
  t.source_system,
  c.legal_name,
  c.country,
  b.desk,
  b.region,
  t.trade_time,
  t.trade_json
FROM trade AS t
LEFT JOIN counterparty FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF t.trade_time AS c
       ON t.counterparty_id = c.counterparty_id
LEFT JOIN book FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF t.trade_time AS b
       ON t.book_id = b.book_id
examples.title: The same feed, enriched

examples.description: Trade processing. Trades arrive all day from half a dozen source systems. A dozen teams want them: the rates desk wants swaps, the equities desk wants equities, risk wants everything from one particular booking system, and settlement wants one trade by id right now.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  t.trade_event_id,
  t.trade_id,
  t.product_type,
  t.source_system,
  t.trade_time,
  t.trade_json
FROM trade AS t
examples.title: Trade processing

examples.description: Cancels. `HOP(event_time, INTERVAL '10' SECOND, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE)` reads as *slide ten seconds, span one minute*. Every event falls into six windows, and the engine slices rather than duplicating: one accumulator per record whatever the overlap, so a sixty-fold overlap does not cost sixty times the memory.
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  HOP_END(o.event_time, INTERVAL '10' SECOND, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE) AS window_end,
  o.trader_id,
  i.symbol,
  COUNT(*) AS cancels
FROM order_event AS o
LEFT JOIN instrument FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.event_time AS i
       ON o.instrument_id = i.instrument_id
WHERE o.event_type = 'CANCEL'
GROUP BY HOP(o.event_time, INTERVAL '10' SECOND, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE), o.trader_id, i.symbol
examples.title: Cancels

examples.description: Orders (Order flow surveillance)
examples.sql:
SELECT STREAM
  HOP_END(o.event_time, INTERVAL '10' SECOND, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE) AS window_end,
  o.trader_id,
  i.symbol,
  i.asset_class,
  COUNT(*)         AS new_orders,
  SUM(o.qty)       AS total_qty,
  MAX(o.price_minor) AS high_price_minor
FROM order_event AS o
LEFT JOIN instrument FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.event_time AS i
       ON o.instrument_id = i.instrument_id
WHERE o.event_type = 'NEW'
GROUP BY HOP(o.event_time, INTERVAL '10' SECOND, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE), o.trader_id, i.symbol, i.asset_class
examples.title: Orders
